pages.title: Introduction to time complexity
pages.content:
Time complexity is a way to measure how long an algorithm takes to run as the amount of **input data** increases. Think of it as a method for figuring out how **fast or slow** an algorithm is.

There are multiple ways to measure time complexity of an algorithm:
1. Best case
2. Average case
3. Worst case

We will focus on understanding the **worst-case scenario** of how an algorithm performs. We use a special notation called “Big O notation” to talk about worst-case time complexity.

#### Why is Time Complexity important?
Time complexity of an algorithm is independent from the machine the algorithm is going to run on. Understanding time complexity is important because it gives us a way of **comparing algorithms** without worrying about the system on which the algorithms are going to run.

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 1
pages.content:
To find out time complexity of an algorithm, we look at the number of operations performed based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the below code:
```python
a = 1
b = 2
print(a + b)
```

In the above algorithm, there is no input. In total three operations are being performed in three lines. Every single operation is denoted as O(1) (pronounced as Big O of 1).

Thus, for the above example, we have time complexity as `O(1) + O(1) + O(1) = 3 * O(1)`

But we denote the time complexity of the above algorithm as O(1), ignoring the constant 3.

#### Rule 1 - Ignore the constants
When calculating time complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

Thus O(1), 5 * O(1), 8 * O(1) are all O(1)

### Task
What will be the time complexity of this algorithm?

```python
a = 4
print(a)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - O(N)
pages.content:
Let's look at another algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
```

In the above algorithm, we are running a loop from 0 to N. In total the loop will run **N** times. For each iteration of the loop we are doing one operation `print(i).

The final time complexity will be: N * O(1) => O(N).

This time the algorithm dependent on a variable N and with that the time complexity also has the value N.

### Task

What if we were doing two operations inside the loop?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
    print(i * 2)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Rule 2
pages.content:
Let's see a different example now.

```python
a = 4 + 5
for i = 0 to N
    print(a)
```

Can you determine the time complexity of this algorithm?

Time complexity of first line => O(1)
Time complexity of the loop => O(N)

Total time complexity => O(1) + O(N).

But can we use two Big Os to define time complexity of an algorithm?
Nope

#### Rule 2 - Focus only on the largest factor
If an algorithm has multiple different parts with different time complexity, when determining the final time complexity we only look at the largest factor.

Because the biggest factor will slow down an algorithm the most.

Thus the time complexity of the above algorithm will be: **O(N)**

### Task
Can you determine final time complexity of the given algorithm, considering the two rules?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to N
    print(j)
```

pages.title: Finding time complexity - Nested loops
pages.content:
Let's take a bit complex algorithm now.
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        print(i)
        print(j)
```

What do you think will the time complexity be?

This is a nested loop. The outer loop runs N times. And for each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop also runs N times.

For each iterations of inner loop there are two operations.

Complexity of line 3 and 4 => O(1) + O(1) => **O(1)**

Total complexity of inner loop => N * (complexity of line 3 and 4) => N * O(1) => **O(N)**

Total complexity of outer loop => N * (complexity of line 2 - 4) => N * O(N) => **O(N * N)**

It can also be represented as **O(N ^ 2)**

Notice how the number of operations are multiplied in case of nested codes.

### Task
Now can you find the complexity of this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    for j = 0 to N
        for k = 0 to N
            print(i)
```

pages.title: Summary of Time Complexity
pages.content:
In this lesson we learned all about Time complexity.

Time complexity is a way to measure how long an algorithm takes to run as the amount of **input data** increases.

We learned about how to find time complexity by counting the number of operations performed in an algorithm.

We also learned about two rules of finding time complexity of an algorithm
1. Ignore constants
2. Focus only on the largest factor

We ignore constants when finding the final time complexity. Also, if there are multiple pieces of an algorithm with varying time complexity, we only take the largest factor.

We also learned how to calculate time complexity of nested loops.

In the next lesson we will see how we have to break the Rule 2 sometimes and also how to apply time complexity to DSA problems in general. 

Then we will practice a lot of problems on finding time complexity.

pages.title: Two loops
pages.content:
We have learned about the basic algorithms and their time complexities in the last few lessons, but there are many different algorithms and thus there can be a lot of different variations in time complexity as well.

See this algorithm:
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to M
    print(j)
```

What do you think will the time complexity be? Let's calculate.

First loop => O(N)  
Second loop => O(M)

Total => **O(N + M)**

But Rule 2 says that we only care about the largest factor no?

We cannot ignore either of N or M because both are variable and we don't know which one is bigger or smaller. So we have to keep both of them in the final complexity.

If we are already given that M is very large as compared to N, then we can say the complexity is O(M). But in general case, it is still **O(N + M)**.

### Task
Now can you think of what the time complexity will be for this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to N
    print(i)

for j = 0 to M
    print(j)

for i = 0 to N
    print(i)
```

pages.title: Time complexity for DSA
pages.content:
We will solve a lot of examples on time complexity, but let’s take a break and think about the applications of time complexity when it comes to solving DSA problems.

Remember how each problem statement on SEED-IT has a **Constraints** section. This section talks about the constraint on the size of input given to you.

The constraints section generally look like this:  
$1 \leq N \leq 10^5$

This means that the value of N can range from 1 to 10^5.

----

For harder problems it is not enough that your solution is correct, it also has to be efficient enough to run within the given time limit.

In general, you can assume that the current day computers can run up to 10 ^ 8 operations per second. You can calculate the worst case time complexity of your algorithm and check if the total number of operations are beyond 10 ^ 8. If the operations performed by your algorithm exceeds 10 ^ 8, you will get TLE or Time limit exceeded.

### Task
What will the number of operations performed by your algorithm be, if maximum value of N can be 10 ^ 6 and time complexity of the algorithm is O(N)?

pages.title: Time complexity of standard algorithms
pages.content:
Hope you have got an idea on how to figure out whether your algorithm will work or give TLE based on the constraints provided.

The steps are - 
1. Find the worst case time complexity of your algorithm
2. Put the maximum possible value of N according to the constraints and check the approximate number of operations
3. If the operations are below $10 ^ 8$, your algorithm can run otherwise it will give TLE.

---

Let's now look at time complexity of some of the standard algorithms. Remembering this numbers help you quickly decide whether you can do that operation or not based on the constraints.

### Loops
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Single loop till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Nested loops both till N | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Two loops one by one till N | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |


### Searching
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Linear search | $O(N)$ | $10 ^ 8$ |
| Binary search | $O(log N)$ | $10 ^ {10 ^ 8}$ |


### Sorting
| Algorithm | Complexity | Max value of N possible | 
|---------- |----------|----------|
| Bubble sort, insertion sort | $O(N ^ 2)$ | $10 ^ 4$ |
| Merge sort | $O(N log N)$ | $10 ^ 7$ |


### Array or list operations
| Algorithm | Complexity |
|---------- |----------|
| Adding an element at the end of a list | $O(1)$ |
| Adding an element at the start of a list | $O(N)$ |
| Counting the occurrences of a number in an array | $O(N)$ |

pages.title: Log N time complexity
pages.content:
Till now we have seen time complexity of loops which run linearly from 1 to N, thus having approximately N number of operations. Even if we are incrementing $i$ by 1, 2 or 10, the constant doesn't really matter.

But there are certain types of loops which do very few operations than N and thus we need other ways to denote their time complexity.

Look at the below code for an example
```python
i = 1
while i <= n:
    print(i)
    i *= 2
```

Here $i$ is getting doubled in each iteration.

For $n = 4$, the iterations will be
```python
1
2
4
```
Only 3 iterations. 

How about $n = 16$?
```python
1
2
4
8
16
```
Only 5 iterations.

**Can we calculate the total number of iterations for any $n$?**  
In each iteration, $i$ is getting doubled, so the values of $i$ will be
$1, 2, 4, 8, \ldots, n$.

If we can count the total number of values of $i$, we will know the time complexity. This is because time complexity is nothing but a measure of the number of operations in an algorithm.

**Now, how do we calculate the total number of iterations?**  
If you observe, all the values of $i$ are of the form $2^x$.  
$2^0, 2^1, 2^2, 2^3, \ldots, 2^x$

The last value will be less than or equal to $n$.

In the above series, we can see, in total, there are $x + 1$ values. Thus, we can say, that there were $x + 1$ iterations of the loop.

**How do we find $x$ then?**  

We know that $2^x \leq n$  

Taking the logarithm on both sides.

$\log_2(2^x) \leq \log_2(n)$  

$\log_2(2^x) \equiv xlog_2(2)$   
$\log_2(2)$ is $1$.

Thus, the equation becomes:  
$x \leq \log_2(n)$

The maximum possible value for $x$ is $\log_2(n)$, and $x$ denotes the maximum number of times the loop will run. Thus, the time complexity of this algorithm will be $\log_2(n)$, as figured out by the total number of operations done in the loop.

----

In general, you can remember that anytime a variable in loop is multiplied by a number greater than 1, the time complexity of the loop will be of the form: $log(n)$.

### Task
What will be the time complexity of this algorithm?

```python
i = 1
while i <= n:
    print(i)
    i *= 3
```

pages.title: Square root N time complexity
pages.content:
Now that we have learned about $log(N)$ time complexity, there is only one other non-linear time complexity which is important to know: $O(sqrt(N))$.

That is the number of operations of an algorithm is approximately $sqrt(N)$.

This is an example of a code with $O(sqrt(n))$ time complexity.
```python
i = 1
while i * i <= n:
    print(i)
    i += 1
```

In this, even though $i$ is incremented by 1 in each iteration, the value of $i$ has to go only till $i * i <= n$.


#### How do we calculate the total number of times the loop is running?
It's simple. The iterations will be: $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, \ldots, x$, until $(x *x) \leq n$.

**Let's solve for $x$:**

Given the condition $x^2 \leq n$, we aim to find the value of $x$ that satisfies this inequality.

1. **Initial inequality:**  
   $x^2 \leq n$

2. **Taking the square root on both sides:**  
   $\sqrt{x^2} \leq \sqrt{n}$

3. **Simplifying:**  
   $x \leq \sqrt{n}$

Thus, the maximum possible value of $x$ can be $\sqrt{n}$, making it the time complexity of the given algorithm.

### Task
What is the complexity of this algorithm?
```python
for i = 0 to n:
   j = 0
   while j * j <= n:
      print(i + j)
      j = j + 1
```

pages.title: Harmonic series
pages.content:
Let's look at another interesting example:
```python
for i = 1 to n
    j = 0
    while j < n:
        j += i 
        print(i + j)
```

To analyze the time complexity of the given code, let's break it down into its two main parts: the outer loop and the inner while loop.

1. **Outer loop**: This loop runs from 1 to $n$, so it iterates $n$ times.

2. **Inner while loop**: The behavior of this loop depends on the value of $i$ from the outer loop. For each iteration of the outer loop, $j$ starts at 0 and increases by $i$ until it reaches or exceeds $n$. This means the number of iterations of the inner loop for each value of $i$ is approximately $\frac{n}{i}$.

To find the total time complexity, we sum the number of iterations of the inner loop over all iterations of the outer loop:

$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i}
$

$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i}$ is the harmonic series which grows logarithmically. Thus, the sum can be approximated as $n \log n$.

Therefore, the time complexity of the given code is $O(n \log n)$.

pages.title: Introduction to Space complexity
pages.content:
Space complexity refers to the amount of **memory or space** an algorithm requires to run as a function of the **input data size**. Alongside time complexity, it is an important aspect of analyzing an algorithm's efficiency.

#### Key Points:

**Space Complexity = Auxiliary Space + Input Space:** This means we consider both the extra memory needed by the algorithm and the memory required for the input data.

**Memory Usage:** This includes the memory for variables, data structures, and function calls.

**Auxiliary Space:** This is the extra memory the algorithm uses, excluding the input data. We mainly focus on this because the input size is usually fixed.

**Big O Notation:** We use this to describe the worst-case space usage of an algorithm.

#### Why It Matters?

Understanding space complexity helps prevent memory issues and ensures that algorithms work efficiently, especially when dealing with large data or limited resources.

pages.title: Finding space complexity
pages.content:
To determine an algorithm's space complexity, we examine the amount of extra memory used based on the input size.

Let's take a look at the following code:
```cpp
int a = 1
int b = 2
cout << a + b;
```
The above algorithm declares two variables *a* and *b*. Each variable takes constant space, which is independent of the input size. Every single variable takes **O(1)** space.

Thus, for the above example, we have the space complexity as:

**O(1) + O(1) = 2 * O(1)**

However, we denote the above algorithm's space complexity as **O(1)**, ignoring the constant 2.

**Ignore the constants**
When calculating space complexity, we ignore the constant values because they don’t matter when the input size becomes large.

**Examine the code below:**
```cpp
cout << "Hello";
```

pages.title: Understanding Space Complexity of Algorithms
pages.content:
When analyzing space complexity, we focus on the amount of memory that an algorithm or data structure requires about the size of the input. The space can be categorized into **input space** (the space taken up by the input data) and **auxiliary space** (the extra memory used by the algorithm for computation).

#### Space Complexity of Common Algorithms
|  *Algorithms*   | *Auxiliary Space* | *Input Space* |
| -------------   | -------------     | -----------   |
| Linear Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Binary Search   |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Selection Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bubble Sort     |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Insertion Sort  |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Merge Sort      |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |
| Quick Sort      |      O(log n)     |    O(n)       |
| Radix Sort      |      O(n+k)       |    O(n)       |
| Counting Sort   |      O(n+m)       |    O(n)       |
| Heap Sort       |      O(1)         |    O(n)       |
| Bucket Sort     |      O(n)         |    O(n)       |

- Quicksort has a space complexity of O(log(n)) in the average case. It can be O(n) due to an unbalanced partitioning leading to a deep recursion stack in the worst case.
- k is the range of input in Radix sort.
- Counting Sort requires O(N+M), where N and M are the space taken by outputArray[] and countArray[] respectively.

pages.title: Trade-Off
pages.content:
#### The trade-off between space and time complexity:
It is basically a problem-solving technique in which we solve a problem :
- Either in less time and using more space, or
- In very little space by spending more time.

The trade-offs between time and space complexity are often *inversely proportional*, meaning that improving one may worsen the other.

The best algorithm is the one that helps to solve a problem that requires less space in memory as well as takes less time to generate the output. But in general, it is not always possible to achieve both of these conditions at the same time.

If a problem is slow but memory-efficient, using more memory can speed it up. Conversely, if a solution is fast but memory-intensive, using less memory might slow it down.

**Example:**  
- Selection sort uses o(n^2) time complexity but no auxiliary space. Space complexity o(1)
- But merge sort uses o(n log n) time complexity and extra O(n) space.
